title: Puritan meditation
hookLine: Richard Baxter taught heavenly meditation: thinking deeply on one truth

lines: A REST TO THE PEOPLE OF GOD.
cards: "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God." One short verse from the letter to the Hebrews. An English Puritan pastor named Richard Baxter built a long book on it, called The Saints' Everlasting Rest.
The story goes that he began it while badly ill and far from home, expecting to die, with little to read but his Bible.
He lived, and the book became a guide to a kind of prayer he called heavenly meditation: taking one truth and thinking it through until it reaches the heart. Today: Puritan meditation.

teach.b: Baxter noticed something in believers, himself included: you can know a truth perfectly well and feel nothing about it. Heaven becomes a doctrine on a shelf.

teach.h: FROM THE HEAD TO THE HEART.
teach.b: Meditation, for him, was carrying a truth from the head down to the heart, work he called consideration. Pick one truth; for Baxter it's usually the rest God promises. Don't skim it.
Turn it over. What is this rest? Who is it for?
What would it be like to be finished with grief and striving? Then let it stir you: love, desire, hope, joy. And when your own heart is slow, talk to it.

teach.h: WHY ART THOU CAST DOWN, O MY SOUL?
teach.b: Baxter calls this soliloquy, preaching to yourself, and he points to the psalmist: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God."
He isn't speaking to God there, or to a friend, but to his own soul, arguing it back toward hope.
The word Hebrews uses for that rest is sabbatismos: a sabbath-keeping. Not a nap. A sabbath, like the rest the letter says God took on the seventh day, now held open for his people.

The Bible's first psalm already blesses this habit: "in his law doth he meditate day and night." In this tradition, meditation isn't emptying the mind. It's filling it with one thing and staying there.
Christians meditate in other ways too, with an image, a single word, or silence. The Puritans kept close to a text, reasoned with it, and talked back to their own hearts.

how: Some Reformed and evangelical Christians meditate in the Puritan way: they choose a verse or a truth, think it through slowly, speak to their own hearts about it, and turn it into prayer, often in a daily quiet time.

o: turning one Bible truth over until it moves the heart
a strict rule of silence kept by Puritans every Sunday
emptying the mind of every thought to find inner calm

p: carrying a truth from head to heart
a sabbath rest for God's people

games.q: you know a truth about God perfectly well, and you feel nothing about it. what does Baxter tell you to do?
o: wait until the feeling comes on its own.
turn it over, let it stir you, and talk to your own heart.
move on to a more exciting truth.
games.why: Baxter calls it consideration: carry the truth from head to heart, and when the heart is slow, preach to it, the way the psalmist asks his soul why it is cast down.

practice: Choose one line, there remaineth a rest to the people of God, or another that matters to you, say it once, and turn it over: what does it say, and what would it mean if it were true for you today?
When your mind wanders, come back to the line, and if your heart feels slow, try Baxter's way and speak to it. If you pray, end by bringing the line to God.

wordCard.voice: Puritan meditation. Taking one truth, like the rest God promises, and thinking it through until it moves from the head to the heart.

orig.note: Greek: a sabbath-keeping, a sabbath rest — the word behind "rest" in Hebrews 4:9.

carryVoice: Your line: the saints' everlasting rest. One truth, from head to heart. Back tomorrow, same hill.
